title: The Last Map on the Wall
subject: rla
passage:
When the travel shop announced it would close, most of the shelves emptied quickly. Suitcases went first, then guidebooks, then the little brass compasses that tourists liked to buy even though their phones already knew north.

I worked there only on Saturdays, but I had spent enough afternoons folding maps to know which drawer stuck in wet weather and which customers would ask for the oldest edition because they liked seeing roads that no longer existed.

On the final morning, Mr. Vale stood beneath the enormous paper map of the city that had hung behind the counter for as long as I could remember. Its corners had curled away from the wall. Colored pins marked hotels, train stations, museums, and a bakery that had closed before I was born.

"That can go in the recycling," I said, pointing up.

Mr. Vale did not answer. He climbed the small ladder and removed the first pin instead. Then another. He placed each one into his palm as if counting coins.

I began packing receipt rolls into a box. "You know the city has changed."

"That's what maps are good at showing," he said.

I looked again. A blue line marked a tram route that had been replaced by buses. A red circle surrounded the old stadium, now an apartment complex. Someone had drawn a tiny star beside the river with a pencil.

"What's that?" I asked.

Mr. Vale squinted. "Your mother put that there."

I laughed because the answer made no sense. My mother hated maps. She used landmarks: turn after the yellow house, stop when you smell bread.

"First week she worked here," he said. "She kept getting lost on deliveries. That star was the only place she could recognize from across the river."

The shop suddenly seemed less empty. I could picture my mother at seventeen, irritated with a folded map, trying to match streets to buildings. I had known she worked for Mr. Vale years ago, but the fact had always sounded like a line from someone else's biography.

Mr. Vale removed the final pin and stepped down. "Still recycling?"

I looked at the faded tram line and the penciled star.

"No," I said. "But I'm not sure it belongs in a box either."

We rolled the map carefully around a cardboard tube. Before I left, Mr. Vale handed it to me with both hands. Outside, my phone buzzed with the quickest route home. I put it back in my pocket and carried the old city under my arm.
